common_name: Feature Attraction Bearded Iris (Lavender-Grape Laced Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun; Schreiner's Gardens introduced this laced lavender-grape iris, registered in 1994, which earned an Award of Merit in 1998 but did not win the AIS Dykes Medal.

directions: Plant rhizomes with the top surface exposed to full sun in well-drained soil, since this vigorous Schreiner introduction is prone to rot in heavy, waterlogged clay. Feature Attraction shows a rich, ruffled lavender-grape self with laced edges and a cool white signal and beard, a refined color combination that earned it an Award of Merit from the American Iris Society. Its tall, well-branched stalks carry many buds in succession, making it a reliable choice for a long bloom display in a mixed perennial border. Lift and divide crowded clumps every three to four years after flowering to keep bloom count high.

common_name: Romantic Evening Bearded Iris (Lilac-Blue and Blackish Red-Purple Bitone Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top exposed, in late summer to early fall; this lilac-blue and blackish red-purple bitone, hybridized by Joseph Ghio and registered in 1994, has not won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal (the 2003 medal went to Schreiner's 'Celebration Song').

directions: Set rhizomes just below the soil surface with the top exposed to full sun in sharply drained ground, since this iris's dense flower substance shows best where roots never sit wet. Romantic Evening carries lilac-blue standards over smooth, velvety blackish red-purple falls with deep brick-colored beards, a dramatic bitone so richly toned that the falls can read almost black-purple in low afternoon light. The heavy ruffling and broad falls make it one of the most photographed dark-toned bearded iris cultivars, and it pairs well against pale yellow or white companions in a border. Divide every three to four years after bloom, discarding the oldest center rhizomes to keep new growth vigorous.

common_name: Point Well Taken Arilbred Iris (Ivory-and-Golden-Tan Blend Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun; this arilbred, hybridized by Sharon McAllister and registered in 1998, has not won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal.

directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally with the top surface uncovered in well-drained soil, giving this arilbred plenty of air movement around the crown to discourage rot. Point Well Taken pairs a pinkish-ivory ground lightly veined in golden yellow on the standards with golden tan falls heavily stippled in rust around a mustard-brown beard, a soft blend pattern typical of quarter-bred arilbred irises. The subtle veining and stippling make it an interesting focal point for collectors assembling an arilbred or oncobred bed. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom finishes to sustain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Blue Shimmer Bearded Iris (Historic 1941 Blue-Stitched Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Jacob Sass registered this white-ground plicata in 1941, and it remains a widely grown heirloom more than eight decades later.

directions: Set rhizomes with the top surface exposed to full sun in lean, sharply drained soil; older heirloom cultivars like this one tend to rot quickly if planted too deep or kept consistently moist. Blue Shimmer bears a white ground stippled and peppered with blue through the center of each fall, a delicate broken-color pattern that was considered strikingly modern when Jacob Sass introduced it in the early 1940s. More than eighty years of continuous commercial availability has made it a benchmark heirloom for gardeners assembling a historic iris collection alongside newer ruffled hybrids. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Ambassadeur Bearded Iris (Historic 1920 French Smoky Lavender-and-Maroon Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top exposed, in late summer to early fall; the Vilmorin nursery of France introduced this smoky lavender-and-maroon bicolor in 1920, one of the influential early-twentieth-century imports that reshaped American iris breeding.

directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, following the same shallow-planting rule that suits all tall bearded iris. Ambassadeur pairs smoky lavender standards with velvety purple-maroon falls, a smoky, saturated bicolor blend that was prized in French gardens of the 1920s and widely exported to American collections during the interwar golden age of iris breeding. Its deep, warm coloring makes it a good companion for the paler heirloom plicatas and blue selfs of the same era in a period border. Divide every three to four years after bloom, since older French heirlooms of this vintage tend to lose vigor if left undivided too long.
sources: Societe Francaise des Iris et Plantes Bulbeuses

common_name: Depute Nomblot Bearded Iris (Historic 1929 Rosy-Bronze and Garnet-Red French Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; the Cayeux firm of France registered this rosy-purple-and-bronze, garnet-red-falled bicolor in 1929.

directions: Set rhizomes with the top surface uncovered in sharply drained soil, since this early French cultivar's compact stature and modest substance make it more susceptible to rot in wet clay than modern hybrids. Depute Nomblot pairs light glowing rosy-purple standards overlaid with bronzy gold against wide, spreading purplish garnet-red falls that shade to a lighter rosy-bronze at the edge, a warm bicolor blend that was among the deepest-toned available in French iris breeding of the late 1920s. It is a good choice for gardeners recreating an authentic period planting of interwar-era French and American tall bearded introductions. Divide every three to four years after bloom to maintain steady flowering, as this heirloom's rhizomes multiply more slowly than modern ramped-up hybrids.
sources: Societe Francaise des Iris et Plantes Bulbeuses

common_name: Gracchus Bearded Iris (Historic 1884 Yellow-and-Crimson Reticulated Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun; Amos Perry of England introduced this yellow-and-crimson iris in 1884, making it one of the oldest tall bearded cultivars still in commercial circulation.

directions: Plant rhizomes with the top surface exposed to full sun in lean, well-drained soil, since this nineteenth-century cultivar predates modern breeding for rot resistance and does best left undisturbed once established. Gracchus displays golden-yellow standards with crimson falls netted and reticulated with white, an antique broken-color pattern that has been continuously grown by heirloom iris collectors since Victorian times. Its shorter stature and smaller flowers compared with modern tall bearded hybrids reflect its nineteenth-century origin, making it a useful reference point for the earliest era of named iris cultivars. Leave clumps undivided for several years, since flowering can be sparse the season immediately after transplanting.

common_name: Jean Cayeux Bearded Iris (Historic 1931 French Golden-Brown Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top exposed, in late summer to early fall; Ferdinand Cayeux introduced this glistening golden-brown iris in 1931, naming it for his grandson.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, giving the crown room to bake dry between waterings as it would in the Loire Valley nurseries where it originated. Jean Cayeux glows with a glistening pale Havana-brown color flushed with gold across both standards and falls, touched with blue venation and beard accents, an unusual warm color combination that distinguished it from the cooler blues and purples common in iris breeding of its era. As one of the enduring Cayeux family introductions of the early 1930s, it remains sought after by collectors building a historic French iris collection. Divide every three to four years after bloom to keep clumps vigorous and free-flowering.
sources: Societe Francaise des Iris et Plantes Bulbeuses

common_name: Indian Chief Bearded Iris (Historic 1929 Ayres Violet-Red Bitone Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun; Cincinnati, Ohio hybridizer Dr. Wylie McLean Ayres registered this violet-red and velvety-red bitone in 1929, part of the broader wave of American breeders pursuing warmer iris tones in that era.

directions: Plant rhizomes with the top surface uncovered in sharply drained soil, since older 1920s-era cultivars are less tolerant of soggy crowns than modern hybrids bred for garden vigor. Indian Chief carries violet-red standards over darker, velvety deep red falls with a bronzy overcast, one of the deeper, warmer red tones American hybridizers pursued as breeding moved away from the blues and violets that had dominated earlier decades. It remains a useful marker of the transitional 1920s breeding period when hybridizers first began chasing red and copper tones in tall bearded iris. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to sustain good flowering.

common_name: Autumn Circus Bearded Iris (1990 White-and-Blue-Violet Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top exposed, in late summer to early fall; Ben Hager registered this white-and-blue-violet plicata in 1990, and it became known as one of the more distinctive reblooming plicata patterns of its era.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to full sun in well-drained soil, allowing the crown to dry between waterings. Autumn Circus pairs white standards lightly peppered in blue-violet to a solid edge with white falls marked by bold lines radiating from the beard and a blue-violet plicata edge, a tetraploid rebloomer whose early-and-fall bloom habit set it apart from single-flush cultivars of its era. Its distinctive reblooming habit and crisp plicata pattern have kept it popular with gardeners seeking extended iris color through the season. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep flowering strong.
